title: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 5 — Every Kid Speaks
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart explains how he moved from believing shy students need not talk to requiring every student to speak almost every day. The shift came from an Amway field trip where in-person communication dominated what employers valued, and from reading Schmoker, Graff and the Common Core speaking and listening standards. He lays out three routines: index cards for random calling so every student speaks each period, think-pair-share as the default collaboration structure with explicitly taught and re-taught procedures, and mandatory participation in whole-class debates and discussions. He answers objections that not everyone needs public speaking, that anxiety harms introverts, and that tests won't assess it, arguing his goal is choice-filled lives rather than producing orators. He reports non-cooperation under 1% and attributes it to rehearsal time, a safe classroom where meanness is unacceptable, modeling failure, grading and quietly logging non-participation. The piece closes by urging nervous teachers to expect participation from every student.
points: Stuart grounds mandatory speaking in employers' emphasis on in-person communication, a skill standardized tests are ill-suited to measure.
A deck of student index cards, worked through each period, is his low-tech guarantee that every student speaks at least once.
Think-pair-share with taught procedures (everyone participates, 'Louder please,' every member can summarize the discussion) gives shy students rehearsal before being called on.
When routines decay he re-teaches the what, why and how, tying the why to college and career readiness or character strengths.
Near-universal participation comes from rehearsal time, a safe no-mockery culture, modeling failure, light grading and not making a scene over refusals.
quotes: Prior to the Common Core, I nurtured a belief that not all of my students needed to talk. After all, some are shy (I was, too, as a secondary school student), and mandatory speaking events can bring about fits of visceral terror for the introverted.

They all seemed to suggest that simply getting every student reading, writing, and talking would do much to prepare students for a diverse array of post-secondary demands. And so it came to be that I grew convinced enough to implement three simple strategies for ensuring every student spoke just about every day.

Whenever it's time to call on students to share their thinking on an issue, a text, or a question I've posed, I use the index cards. If I can work through a deck each class period, I have ensured that every student has spoken at least once.
My goal isn't to create classes of public speakers, but it is to enable my students to live choice-filled lives. If they choose to pursue professions that require no public speaking, great!
I am vigilant in creating a safe space for my students. Meanness is out of place and unacceptable. My students know they won't be mocked for not having it all together.

I model the value of failure. My students know that those who deliberately practice in their areas of weakness have a huge advantage over those who don't. They know that I am the most expert failer in the room because I've failed the most and I aggressively learn from failure.
Yet, as I look at my students and how they've grown in confidence and skill, I'm thankful I dared to expect every one of them to participate in each of our speaking/listening events.
